question: Why would programmers struggle if computers had no OS?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: They would have to work directly with the CPU, memory, disk and I/O devices, needing detailed hardware knowledge; portability would be very limited.

gold_quotes.quote: application developers would need to directly interact with hardware components such as the CPU, memory, disk, and I/O devices
Hardware knowledge would be mandatory for programming • Software portability would be extremely limited

question: What does the bootstrap program do?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: It initializes CPU registers, memory and device controllers, and loads the OS kernel into memory.

gold_quotes.quote: Functions of bootstrap: • Initializes CPU registers • Initializes memory • Initializes device controllers
Loads the operating system kernel into memory

question: How do handheld devices and embedded systems differ in what the OS is designed for?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: Handheld devices are resource-constrained and optimized for battery life and usability; embedded systems often have little or no user interface.

gold_quotes.quote: Handheld devices: Resource-constrained, optimized for: o Battery life o Usability
Embedded systems: Often have little or no user interface

question: What hardware parts make up a computer system's organization?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: One or more CPUs, device controllers, shared main memory and a common system bus.

gold_quotes.quote: A computer system consists of: • One or more CPUs
Device controllers • Shared main memory • Common system bus

question: What is the job of the memory controller?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: CPU and device controllers run concurrently and compete for memory cycles; the memory controller synchronizes access to shared memory.

gold_quotes.quote: The CPU and device controllers can execute concurrently, competing for memory cycles. A memory controller synchronizes access to shared memory.

question: How does the computer figure out which device caused an interrupt?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: By polling, or with a vectored interrupt system that uses an interrupt vector of service-routine addresses.

gold_quotes.quote: Interrupt identification methods: • Polling • Vectored interrupt systems
Uses an interrupt vector containing addresses of service routines

question: What are the characteristics of secondary storage?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: It extends main memory, is non-volatile and has large capacity.

gold_quotes.quote: Secondary storage: • Extension of main memory • Non-volatile • Large capacity

question: What are the challenges in caching?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: Cache size, replacement policy and cache management.

gold_quotes.quote: Challenges: • Cache size • Replacement policy • Cache management

question: Can the computer keep running my program while a printer is busy printing?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: Yes, in the second I/O model the CPU continues execution while I/O proceeds, and resumes after the completion interrupt.

gold_quotes.quote: Two models: 1. CPU waits for I/O completion 2. CPU continues execution while I/O proceeds
CPU resumes execution after I/O completion interrupt

question: What does the OS do as a resource allocator?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: It manages all system resources, resolves conflicting requests and ensures fairness and efficiency.

gold_quotes.quote: Resource Allocator o Manages all system resources o Resolves conflicting resource requests o Ensures fairness and efficiency

question: Why should I learn OS concepts if I will never build an operating system?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: Almost all software runs on top of an OS, so OS knowledge helps write efficient and secure programs and debug performance issues.

gold_quotes.quote: Although only a small percentage of computer professionals design or modify operating systems, almost all software runs on top of an OS.
Writing efficient programs • Developing secure applications

question: Where is EEPROM used?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: In smartphones, to store factory-installed programs; it also stores the bootstrap program.

gold_quotes.quote: EEPROM (used in smartphones to store factory-installed programs)

question: What is the main objective of multiprogramming?
reference_answer: To keep the CPU busy at all times and maximize CPU utilization.

gold_quotes.quote: The main objective of multiprogramming is to: • Keep the CPU busy at all times • Maximize CPU utilization

question: How is CPU scheduling done on a multicore system?
reference_answer: Each core should be kept busy and scheduling decisions are made independently for each core.

gold_quotes.quote: On a multicore system, the same concept is extended: • Each processing core should be kept busy • Scheduling decisions are made independently for each core

question: What is the difference between a CPU burst and an I/O burst?
reference_answer: In a CPU burst the process executes instructions; in an I/O burst it waits for I/O completion.

gold_quotes.quote: CPU burst → process is executing instructions • I/O burst → process is waiting for I/O completion

question: Do programs that mostly read and write files use the processor in short or long stretches?
reference_answer: They are I/O-bound, so they have many short CPU bursts; CPU-bound processes have few long bursts.

gold_quotes.quote: I/O-bound processes o Many short CPU bursts • CPU-bound processes o Few long CPU bursts
I/O-Bound Process o Spends more time doing I/O o Many short CPU bursts

question: In what ways can the ready queue be organized?
reference_answer: As a FIFO queue, priority queue, tree or unordered linked list; each entry is a PCB.

gold_quotes.quote: The ready queue may be organized in various ways: • FIFO queue • Priority queue • Tree • Unordered linked list

question: What are the functions of the dispatcher?
reference_answer: It performs the context switch, switches to user mode and jumps to the right location in the user program.

gold_quotes.quote: Dispatcher Functions • Performs context switch • Switches CPU to user mode • Jumps to the correct location in the user program

question: What is dispatch latency?
reference_answer: The time taken by the dispatcher to stop one process and start another; an important performance metric.

gold_quotes.quote: Dispatch Latency • Time taken to: o Stop one process
o Start another process • Important performance metric

question: Which operating systems used non-preemptive scheduling and which used preemptive?
reference_answer: Windows 3.x was non-preemptive; Windows 95 onwards and Macintosh OS are preemptive.

gold_quotes.quote: Windows 3.x → Non-preemptive • Windows 95 onwards → Preemptive • Macintosh OS → Uses preemptive scheduling

question: Which measure matters most when users are typing and waiting for the screen to react?
reference_answer: Response time: time from request submission to first response, important in time-sharing systems.

gold_quotes.quote: Time from request submission to first response o Important in time-sharing systems

question: What should a good scheduler try to keep as small as possible?
reference_answer: Turnaround time, waiting time and response time.

gold_quotes.quote: Minimize o Turnaround time o Waiting time o Response time

question: What are the sections of a process in memory?
reference_answer: Text section, current activity (program counter and registers), stack, data section and heap.

gold_quotes.quote: A process consists of several parts in memory: 1. Text Section o Program code
Stack o Temporary data o Function parameters o Return addresses o Local variables 4. Data Section o Global and static variables
Heap o Dynamically allocated memory during runtime

question: Where do a function's local variables live while the program runs?
reference_answer: On the stack, together with temporary data, function parameters and return addresses.

gold_quotes.quote: Stack o Temporary data o Function parameters o Return addresses o Local variables

question: What states can a process be in?
reference_answer: New, running, waiting, ready and terminated.

gold_quotes.quote: Common Process States 1. New o Process is being created 2. Running o Instructions are currently being executed 3. Waiting
Ready o Process is waiting to be assigned to a CPU 5. Terminated o Process has finished execution

question: How is the long-term scheduler different from the short-term scheduler?
reference_answer: The short-term scheduler picks the next process for the CPU and runs every few milliseconds; the long-term scheduler admits processes into the ready queue, runs every few seconds or minutes and controls the degree of multiprogramming.

gold_quotes.quote: Short-Term Scheduler (CPU Scheduler) • Selects the next process to execute on the CPU • Invoked very frequently (milliseconds)
Long-Term Scheduler (Job Scheduler) • Selects processes to be admitted into the ready queue • Invoked infrequently (seconds or minutes)

question: What is swapping and why is it used?
reference_answer: The medium-term scheduler removes a process from memory to disk and brings it back later, to reduce the degree of multiprogramming.

gold_quotes.quote: A medium-term scheduler may be introduced to: • Reduce the degree of multiprogramming Swapping
is removed from memory • Stored on disk • Later brought back to continue execution

question: Which scheduling queues does the operating system maintain?
reference_answer: The job queue (all processes), the ready queue (in memory, ready to run) and device queues (waiting for I/O).

gold_quotes.quote: The operating system maintains several scheduling queues: 1. Job Queue
All processes in the system 2. Ready Queue o Processes in main memory o Ready to execute 3. Device Queues o Processes waiting for I/O devices

question: When can a parent process terminate its child?
reference_answer: Using abort() when the child exceeds its resources, its task is no longer needed, or the parent is itself terminating.

gold_quotes.quote: Parent may terminate a child using abort() if: • Child exceeds allocated resources • Task assigned to child is no longer needed • Parent itself is terminating

question: What is cascading termination?
reference_answer: In systems that do not allow a child without a parent, when the parent terminates all its children are terminated by the OS.

gold_quotes.quote: Some operating systems do not allow a child to exist without a parent.
all children terminate • This is called cascading termination • Initiated by the operating system

question: How does a parent find out how its child ended?
reference_answer: The child returns a status value, which the parent retrieves with wait().

gold_quotes.quote: Status value returned from child to parent • Parent retrieves status using wait()

question: What are the options for sharing resources between parent and child processes?
reference_answer: They share all resources, the child shares a subset of the parent's resources, or they share none.

gold_quotes.quote: Resource Sharing Options • Parent and child share all resources • Child shares
a subset of parent’s resources • Parent and child share no resources
